claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr contains approximately 20 at.% each of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
Chemical complexity in equimolar WTaTiVZr produces significant lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr lowers the effective Peierls barrier for dislocation motion.
The reduced effective barrier promotes enhanced dislocation cross-slip in WTaTiVZr at high temperature.
The reduced effective barrier promotes enhanced dislocation climb in WTaTiVZr at high temperature.
Enhanced cross-slip and climb produce more spatially distributed plastic deformation.
More distributed plastic deformation reduces stress concentrations.
The proposed dislocation behavior gives WTaTiVZr higher high-temperature plastic strain than pure tungsten.
The proposed dislocation behavior gives WTaTiVZr greater high-temperature toughness than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will undergo more deformation before failure than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit less crack propagation than pure tungsten.
Post-deformation TEM will reveal a more dynamic and widespread dislocation network in WTaTiVZr than in pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a higher Peierls barrier than WTaTiVZr under the proposed conditions.
Pure tungsten exhibits greater dislocation pinning and more limited dislocation mobility than WTaTiVZr.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism dominates above approximately 900 °C because thermal energy is sufficient to activate dislocation motion.
Below approximately 900 °C, the effect of lattice distortion on plasticity is less pronounced because thermal activation is reduced.
Matching grain size and initial defect content between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten is intended to control microstructural confounders.
Grain-boundary effects or minor precipitates could influence measured differences in plastic strain and toughness.
Testing from 900 °C to 1500 °C under controlled strain rates represents high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions.
